cards.englishPhrase: Which direction is the station?
cards.phrase: ¿En qué dirección está la estación?

cards.grammarNote:
**En** covers both *in* and *at* for location: **en la bolsa** (in the bag), **en la oficina** (at the office), **en el aeropuerto** (at the airport).
**Las llaves están en la bolsa** — location uses **estar**. **Las llaves** (the keys) is feminine plural.
Contrast **en** (location/state) with **a** (direction/destination): **Estoy en casa** vs **Voy a casa**.
cards.englishPhrase: The keys are in the bag.
cards.phrase: Las llaves están en la bolsa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Sobre** = on top of / above / about. **El libro está sobre la mesa** = The book is on the table.
**Encima de** is a near-synonym meaning *on top of*: **encima de la mesa** — slightly more emphatic about vertical position.
**En** can also mean *on* in some contexts: **en la mesa** (on the table) is equally natural and very common.
cards.englishPhrase: The book is on the table.
cards.phrase: El libro está sobre la mesa.

cards.grammarNote:
Spanish uses **en** for both *in* and *at* with locations: **Estoy en la oficina** = I'm at/in the office.
**Estoy** is from **estar** — always use **estar** (not **ser**) for location.
The key contrast: **en** (being somewhere) vs **a** (going somewhere): **Estoy en el banco** (I'm at the bank) vs **Voy al banco** (I'm going to the bank).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm at the office.
cards.phrase: Estoy en la oficina.

cards.grammarNote:
**Debajo de** = under/below. Always two words, always followed by **de**.
**Debajo de la mesa** — **de + la** stays as **de la** (no contraction needed; contractions only apply to **de + el**).
Compare position prepositions: **encima de** (on top of) · **debajo de** (under) · **al lado de** (next to) · **delante de** (in front of) · **detrás de** (behind).
cards.englishPhrase: The cat is under the table.
cards.phrase: El gato está debajo de la mesa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Al lado de** = next to / beside. Broken down: **al** (= **a + el**) + **lado** (side) + **de** (of).
**Al lado del café** — **del** = **de + el** (mandatory contraction). The phrase contains *two* contractions: **al** and **del**.
Other position prepositions follow the same **[prep] + de** pattern: **cerca de**, **lejos de**, **delante de**, **detrás de**, **encima de**, **debajo de**.
cards.englishPhrase: The bank is next to the cafe.
cards.phrase: El banco está al lado del café.

cards.grammarNote:
**Entre** = between (two things) or among (more than two). Unlike most position words, it does NOT need **de**: **entre la escuela y la biblioteca** (not *entre de*).
**El parque está entre...** — location uses **estar**.
**Y** = and. Before words starting with **i** or **hi**, **y** changes to **e**: **padre e hijo** (father and son).
cards.englishPhrase: The park is between the school and the library.
cards.phrase: El parque está entre la escuela y la biblioteca.

cards.grammarNote:
**En frente de** = in front of. Also written as **enfrente de** (one word). Both are correct.
**En frente del hotel** — **del** = **de + el** (mandatory contraction).
Compare: **delante de** (physically in front of, e.g., leading the way) vs **enfrente de** (facing/opposite, e.g., across the street).
cards.englishPhrase: The taxi is in front of the hotel.
cards.phrase: El taxi está en frente del hotel.

cards.grammarNote:
**Detrás de** = behind. Always followed by **de**.
**Detrás de la casa** — **de + la** = **de la** (no contraction; only **de + el** contracts to **del**).
Position preposition family: **delante de** (in front of) · **detrás de** (behind) · **encima de** (on top of) · **debajo de** (under) · **al lado de** (next to) · **enfrente de** (facing).
cards.englishPhrase: The garden is behind the house.
cards.phrase: El jardín está detrás de la casa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Cerca de** = near. **Cerca de aquí** = near here. When followed by a masculine noun: **cerca del banco** (del = de + el).
**¿Hay un restaurante cerca de aquí?** — **hay** (there is) introduces new/indefinite information. Compare: **¿Dónde está el restaurante?** (where is the [specific] restaurant — **está** for known/specific).
**Cerca** alone (no **de**) = nearby: **¿Hay una farmacia cerca?**
cards.englishPhrase: Is there a restaurant near here?
cards.phrase: ¿Hay un restaurante cerca de aquí?

cards.grammarNote:
**Lejos de** = far from. Opposite of **cerca de** (near).
**¿Está lejos el aeropuerto?** — inverted word order for questions is natural in Spanish (subject after verb). **El aeropuerto** = **el** + masculine noun.
**El aeropuerto** — etymology: **aero** (air) + **puerto** (port). The same compound in English: *air + port*.
cards.englishPhrase: Is the airport far?
cards.phrase: ¿Está lejos el aeropuerto?

cards.grammarNote:
Three words for 'here': **aquí** (here, right at this spot — most common), **acá** (here, more general — common in Latin America), **aca** (informal variant).
**Ven aquí** — **Ven** is the irregular informal imperative of **venir**. Formal: **Venga aquí**.
**Por favor** = please (literally 'by/for favour'). Always a polite addition when making requests.
cards.englishPhrase: Come here, please.
cards.phrase: Ven aquí, por favor.

cards.grammarNote:
Three words for 'there': **aquí** (here) · **allí** (there, at a specific spot) · **allá** (over there, more vague/distant).
**El taxi está allí** — location uses **estar**.
**Allí mismo** = right there (very precise); **allá lejos** = way over there (distant). The distinction between **allí** and **allá** mirrors **aquí** vs **acá**.
cards.englishPhrase: The taxi is over there.
cards.phrase: El taxi está allí.

cards.grammarNote:
**A la izquierda** = to the left. The full direction phrase always uses **a + la** because **izquierda** is feminine.
**Gira a la izquierda** (turn left) — one of the three essential direction commands alongside **a la derecha** (right) and **todo recto** (straight ahead).
Remember: **izquierda** and **derecha** are nouns (feminine), not adjectives. That's why they take an article: **a la izquierda**, not *a izquierda*.
cards.englishPhrase: Turn left.
cards.phrase: Gira a la izquierda.

cards.grammarNote:
**A la derecha** = to the right. Like **izquierda**, **derecha** is a feminine noun and always takes **a + la**.
**Gira a la derecha** (turn right) · **Gira a la izquierda** (turn left) · **Ve todo recto** (go straight).
**Derecho/a** (adjective) = straight: **todo recto** or **todo derecho**. Don't confuse **derecha** (direction: right) with **derecho** (straight ahead or the noun 'right/law').
cards.englishPhrase: Turn right.
cards.phrase: Gira a la derecha.

cards.grammarNote:
**Todo recto** = straight ahead (literally 'all straight'). Both **todo recto** and **todo derecho** are used — **todo recto** is slightly more common in directions.
**Ve todo recto** — **Ve** is the irregular informal imperative of **ir** (to go). Formal: **Vaya todo recto**.
This completes the trio of essential direction phrases: **a la derecha** · **a la izquierda** · **todo recto**.
cards.englishPhrase: Go straight ahead.
cards.phrase: Ve todo recto.

cards.grammarNote:
**Al norte** = to the north. The contraction **al** = **a + el** is used even with compass directions since they are treated as masculine nouns.
All four cardinal directions are masculine: **el norte**, **el sur**, **el este**, **el oeste**.
Compass direction phrases: **al norte** (to/in the north), **al sur** (south), **al este** (east), **al oeste** (west).
cards.englishPhrase: The city is to the north.
cards.phrase: La ciudad está al norte.

cards.grammarNote:
**Al sur** = to the south. **Al** = **a + el** (mandatory contraction — **sur** is masculine).
**La playa está al sur** — location with **estar**. The beach is located (permanently, for this context) to the south.
Cardinal directions: **norte** · **sur** · **este** · **oeste** — all masculine, all use **al** when saying 'to the [direction]'.
cards.englishPhrase: The beach is to the south.
cards.phrase: La playa está al sur.

cards.grammarNote:
**El este** = the east (masculine). **Por el este** = through/via the east — **por** indicates movement through a direction.
**Sale por el este** — **salir por** = to come out through. The sun 'comes out' (**sale**) through the east.
Beware of homonyms: **este** (east, noun, no accent) · **este** (this, demonstrative adjective, no accent) · **éste** (this one, demonstrative pronoun — accent optional in modern Spanish).
cards.englishPhrase: The sun rises in the east.
cards.phrase: El sol sale por el este.

cards.grammarNote:
**El oeste** = the west (masculine). **En el oeste** = in the west.
**Se pone** — **ponerse** (to set, for the sun) is reflexive. The reflexive **se** signals an automatic/natural process. **El sol se pone** (the sun sets) · **el sol sale** (the sun rises).
**Poner** also means 'to put/place': context distinguishes. Reflexive **ponerse** = to put on (clothing) or to set (sun).
cards.englishPhrase: The sun sets in the west.
cards.phrase: El sol se pone en el oeste.

cards.grammarNote:
**Cerca** (no **de**) = nearby (standalone adverb, no specific reference).
**Cerca de** + noun = near [something]: **cerca de aquí** (near here), **cerca del banco** (near the bank — **del** = de + el).
**¿Hay una farmacia cerca?** — **hay** (there is/are) introduces indefinite existence. If you already know a specific pharmacy: **¿Dónde está la farmacia?** (Where is the pharmacy?).
cards.englishPhrase: Is there a pharmacy nearby?
cards.phrase: ¿Hay una farmacia cerca?

cards.grammarNote:
**Ir** is highly irregular. Present tense: **voy**, **vas**, **va**, **vamos**, **vais**, **van**.
**Ir a + place** = to go to a place: **voy al supermercado**, **voy a casa**, **voy a la playa**.
**Ir a + infinitive** also expresses future: **voy a comer** (I'm going to eat), **vamos a salir** (we're going to leave).
**Al** = **a + el** (mandatory contraction) whenever the destination has a masculine article.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going to the supermarket.
cards.phrase: Voy al supermercado.

cards.grammarNote:
**Venir** is irregular. Present tense: **vengo**, **vienes**, **viene**, **venimos**, **venís**, **vienen**.
**Ven a mi casa** — **Ven** is the informal (tú) imperative.
**Venir a + place** = to come to a place. Contrast: **ir** (to go, away from speaker) vs **venir** (to come, towards speaker) — same speaker-relative logic as English.
cards.englishPhrase: Come to my house.
cards.phrase: Ven a mi casa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Me encanta viajar** — **encantar** works like **gustar**: the subject is the thing loved (**viajar**), not the person. **Me** = indirect object (to me). Literally: 'travelling enchants me'.
Single thing/verb: **me encanta** · Multiple things: **me encantan los viajes**.
**Viajar** is a regular **-ar** verb: viajo, viajas, viaja, viajamos, viajáis, viajan.
cards.englishPhrase: I love to travel.
cards.phrase: Me encanta viajar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Camino al trabajo** — **al** = **a + el** (mandatory contraction before masculine noun **trabajo**).
**Caminar** is a regular **-ar** verb. Also common: **andar** (to walk/go on foot) — more colloquial in Spain.
**Todos los días** = every day (literally 'all the days'). Compare: **cada día** (each day) — both are common and interchangeable.
cards.englishPhrase: I walk to work every day.
cards.phrase: Camino al trabajo todos los días.

cards.grammarNote:
**Manejar** = to drive (Latin America). In Spain: **conducir** (irregular: conduzco, conduces…).
**Maneja a la oficina** — **a la** because **oficina** is feminine. Compare masculine: **al trabajo** (to work), **al banco** (to the bank).
**Ella** (she) is optional — Spanish drops subject pronouns since verb endings identify the subject.
cards.englishPhrase: She drives to the office.
cards.phrase: Ella maneja a la oficina.

cards.grammarNote:
**Gira a la izquierda** — the three core direction commands:
**Gira a la derecha** (turn right) · **Gira a la izquierda** (turn left) · **Ve todo recto** (go straight ahead).
**Gira** is the informal (tú) imperative of **girar**. Formal (usted): **Gire a la izquierda**.
Alternative: **doblar** — **dobla a la derecha** is equally natural.
cards.englishPhrase: Turn left at the corner.
cards.phrase: Gira a la izquierda en la esquina.

cards.grammarNote:
**Cruza la calle** — **Cruza** is the informal (tú) imperative of **cruzar**. Formal: **Cruce la calle**.
**Con cuidado** = carefully (literally 'with care'). **Cuidado** is also used as a standalone warning: **¡Cuidado!** = Watch out!
**Cruzar** is a regular **-ar** verb: cruzo, cruzas, cruza… Note spelling change in preterite (yo): **crucé** (not *cruzé*).
cards.englishPhrase: Cross the street carefully.
cards.phrase: Cruza la calle con cuidado.

cards.grammarNote:
**Sigue esta calle** — **Sigue** is the informal (tú) imperative of **seguir**. Formal: **Siga esta calle**.
**Seguir** is irregular: **sigo**, sigues, sigue, seguimos, seguís, siguen (yo form has irregular **g**).
**Seguir + gerund** = to keep doing something: **sigue recto** (keep going straight), **sigue caminando** (keep walking).
cards.englishPhrase: Follow this street.
cards.phrase: Sigue esta calle.

cards.grammarNote:
**Entra por la puerta** — **entrar por** = to enter through. The preposition is **por** (through/by way of), not **en**.
**Entrar en** is also used (especially in Spain): **entra en el edificio** (enter the building). Latin American Spanish often omits **en**: **entra al edificio**.
**La puerta principal** — **principal** = main. Adjectives follow the noun in Spanish.
cards.englishPhrase: Enter through the main door.
cards.phrase: Entra por la puerta principal.

cards.grammarNote:
**Salir** is irregular in yo: **salgo** (I leave/go out). Other forms are regular: sales, sale, salimos, salís, salen.
**Salgo del trabajo** — **del** = **de + el** (mandatory contraction). You can never write *de el trabajo*.
**A las cinco** = at five (o'clock). Time expressions use **a las** (feminine plural) because **hora** (hour) is feminine: **a la una**, **a las dos**, **a las cinco**.
cards.englishPhrase: I leave work at five.
cards.phrase: Salgo del trabajo a las cinco.

cards.grammarNote:
**Llegar** = to arrive. Regular **-ar** verb (with a spelling change in preterite yo: **llegué**).
**Llegamos mañana** — **llegamos** is both present (we arrive) and preterite (we arrived) for nosotros; **mañana** (tomorrow) here confirms it's present/future.
**Llegar a** + place = to arrive at: **llegamos a Madrid**, **llegamos al hotel** (**al** = a + el).
cards.englishPhrase: We arrive tomorrow.
cards.phrase: Llegamos mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Quiero visitar el museo** — **querer + infinitive** expresses wanting to do something.
**Visitar** is a regular **-ar** verb: visito, visitas, visita, visitamos, visitáis, visitan.
**Visitar** takes a direct object with no preposition: **visitar el museo**, **visitar a un amigo** (personal 'a' before a person — **a** before a specific human direct object is mandatory in Spanish).
cards.englishPhrase: I want to visit the museum.
cards.phrase: Quiero visitar el museo.

cards.grammarNote:
**Vivir** = to live. Regular **-ir** verb: **vivo**, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven.
**Vivo cerca del centro** — **del** = **de + el** (mandatory contraction). **Cerca de** = near.
**Vivir en** = to live in/at a place. **Vivo en Madrid**, **vivo en un apartamento**, **vivo cerca del centro**.
cards.englishPhrase: I live near the city centre.
cards.phrase: Vivo cerca del centro.

cards.grammarNote:
**Quedarse** = to stay/remain (reflexive). The phrase uses **hospedarse** instead — a more specific word meaning to lodge/stay as a guest.
**Nos hospedamos** — reflexive verb with **nos** (we). **Hospedarse** comes from Latin **hospes** (host/guest) — same root as **hospital**, **hotel**, **hostal**.
**Quedarse en** = to stay at: **me quedo en el hotel** (I'm staying at the hotel).
cards.englishPhrase: We're staying at a hotel.
cards.phrase: Nos hospedamos en un hotel.

cards.grammarNote:
**Te espero** = I'll wait for you. **Esperar a alguien** = to wait for someone — the 'for' is built into the verb; no preposition needed before the person.
**Te** = you (indirect object pronoun, informal). Formal: **Le espero**.
**Esperar** also means *to hope*: **espero que llegues pronto** (I hope you arrive soon). Context distinguishes.
cards.englishPhrase: I'll wait for you here.
cards.phrase: Te espero aquí.

cards.grammarNote:
**Quedamos en el parque** uses **quedar** (to arrange to meet) — very natural in Spain for planned meetings.
**Quedar en** = to meet at (a place). Alternative: **encontrarse en**: **nos encontramos en el parque**.
**Quedar** has many meanings: to remain (**queda poco tiempo** = little time remains), to fit (**te queda bien** = it suits you), to arrange to meet (**quedamos a las tres** = let's meet at three).
cards.englishPhrase: Let's meet at the park.
cards.phrase: Quedamos en el parque.

cards.grammarNote:
**Perderse** is reflexive — the pronoun changes with the subject:
**me pierdo** · **te pierdes** · **se pierde**
Many movement/location verbs are reflexive: **quedarse** (to stay), **hospedarse** (to lodge), **dirigirse** (to head)
**¡No te pierdas!** = Don't get lost!
cards.englishPhrase: Don't get lost!
cards.phrase: ¡No te pierdas!

cards.grammarNote:
**No encuentro el hotel** — **encontrar** is a stem-changing verb (o→ue): **encuentro**, encuentras, encuentra, encontramos, encontráis, encuentran.
**No encuentro** = I can't find / I don't find. Spanish present tense covers the English 'can't find' in this context.
Contrast: **encontrar** (to find something) vs **encontrarse** (reflexive: to be located, or to meet someone).
cards.englishPhrase: I can't find the hotel.
cards.phrase: No encuentro el hotel.

cards.grammarNote:
**Busco la farmacia** — **buscar** means 'to look for'. The 'for' is already inside the verb — never add **por** or **para**: say **busco el hotel**, not *busco por el hotel*.
**Buscar** is a regular **-ar** verb (with spelling change in preterite yo: **busqué**).
**La farmacia** — feminine noun. Pharmacies in Spanish-speaking countries are marked by a green cross.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm looking for the pharmacy.
cards.phrase: Busco la farmacia.

cards.grammarNote:
**Para en la esquina** — **Para** is the informal (tú) imperative of **parar** (to stop). Formal: **Pare en la esquina**.
**Parar** (transitive) = to stop something; **pararse** (reflexive) = to stop oneself/come to a stop.
Also common: **detenerse** = to stop (slightly more formal): **detente aquí** (stop here).
cards.englishPhrase: Stop at the corner.
cards.phrase: Para en la esquina.

cards.grammarNote:
**Aparcar** (Spain) / **estacionar** (Latin America) = to park a vehicle. Both are correct.
**¿Dónde puedo estacionar?** — **poder + infinitive** = to be able to / can. **Puedo** is the yo form (stem-changing: o→ue): **puedo**, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden.
**Dónde** = where (with accent in questions). Without accent: **donde** = where (in relative clauses).
cards.englishPhrase: Where can I park?
cards.phrase: ¿Dónde puedo estacionar?

cards.grammarNote:
**El mercado está muy concurrido** — use **estar** (not **ser**) because crowdedness is a temporary state.
**Concurrido** agrees with the subject: **mercado concurrido** (m.) · **calle concurrida** (f.) · **lugares concurridos** (m.pl.) · **calles concurridas** (f.pl.).
Alternatives: **lleno** (full) · **animado** (lively) · **transitado** (busy with traffic).
cards.englishPhrase: The market is very crowded.
cards.phrase: El mercado está muy concurrido.

cards.grammarNote:
**Prefiero un barrio tranquilo** — **tranquilo** = quiet/calm. It follows the noun it modifies (adjectives usually follow in Spanish).
**Tranquilo** agrees with the noun: **barrio tranquilo** (m.) · **calle tranquila** (f.) · **lugares tranquilos** (m.pl.).
**Prefiero** = I prefer (stem-changing verb e→ie): prefiero, prefieres, prefiere, preferimos, preferís, prefieren.
cards.englishPhrase: I prefer a quiet neighbourhood.
cards.phrase: Prefiero un barrio tranquilo.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estoy perdido** — use **estar** (not **ser**) because being lost is a temporary state.
**Perdido** (m.) / **perdida** (f.) — the adjective agrees with the subject: **estoy perdido** (male speaker) · **estoy perdida** (female speaker).
Related: **perderse** (to get lost — reflexive): **me perdí** (I got lost) · **¡No te pierdas!** (Don't get lost!)
cards.englishPhrase: I'm lost.
cards.phrase: Estoy perdido.

cards.grammarNote:
Use **ser** for professions — and omit the article:
**Soy médico** ✓ (not *Soy un médico*) · **Es enfermera** · **Es ingeniero**
The article returns only when the noun is modified: **Soy un buen médico**
cards.englishPhrase: He is a doctor.
cards.phrase: Es médico.

cards.grammarNote:
Gender forms: **el enfermero** (male nurse) / **la enfermera** (female nurse).
From Latin **infirmus** (sick/weak) — compare English "infirmary".
Use **ser** for the profession without an article: **Es enfermera** (She is a nurse).
cards.englishPhrase: She is a nurse.
cards.phrase: Ella es enfermera.

cards.grammarNote:
Gender forms: **el ingeniero** / **la ingeniera**.
From Latin **ingenium** (cleverness, talent, natural ability) — the same root as English "engine" and "ingenious".
Use **ser** without an article: **Mi hermano es ingeniero** (My brother is an engineer).
cards.englishPhrase: My brother is an engineer.
cards.phrase: Mi hermano es ingeniero.

cards.grammarNote:
Gender forms: **el programador** / **la programadora**.
**Trabajo como programador** uses **como** (as/like) — an alternative to **ser**: **soy programador** and **trabajo como programador** both work.
**Trabajar como** is especially natural when describing a current role rather than a permanent identity.
cards.englishPhrase: I work as a programmer.
cards.phrase: Trabajo como programador.

cards.grammarNote:
Gender forms: **el cocinero** / **la cocinera**.
Note the double meaning of **cocina**: it means both "kitchen" (the room) and "cooking/cuisine" (the activity).
**La cocina italiana** = Italian cuisine · **trabajar en la cocina** = to work in the kitchen.
A professional chef is often called **el/la chef** (borrowed from French).
cards.englishPhrase: The cook works in the kitchen.
cards.phrase: El cocinero trabaja en la cocina.

cards.grammarNote:
Gender forms: **el camarero** / **la camarera** (Spain).
In Latin America you'll often hear **el mesero / la mesera** instead.
**Trajo** is the preterite (past tense) of **traer** (to bring) — an irregular verb: traje, trajiste, trajo, trajimos, trajeron.
Note the accent on **menú** — required because the stress falls on the final syllable.
cards.englishPhrase: The waiter brought the menu.
cards.phrase: El camarero trajo el menú.

cards.grammarNote:
**Gerente** is a shared-gender noun: **el gerente** / **la gerente** (the ending doesn't change).
This is common with nouns ending in **-ente** or **-ante**: **el/la estudiante**, **el/la presidente**, **el/la asistente**.
Another word for manager: **el/la director(a)** (director), **el/la jefe/jefa** (boss/chief).
cards.englishPhrase: She is a manager.
cards.phrase: Ella es gerente.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estudiante** is a shared-gender noun: **el estudiante** / **la estudiante** — the word itself doesn't change.
This is typical of nouns ending in **-nte**: **el/la asistente**, **el/la presidente**, **el/la gerente**.
Use **ser** without an article for professions/roles: **Soy estudiante** (I am a student) — not *Soy un estudiante*.
cards.englishPhrase: I am a student.
cards.phrase: Soy estudiante.

cards.grammarNote:
Gender forms: **el arquitecto** / **la arquitecta**.
From Greek **arkhitekton** (master builder): **arkhi-** (chief) + **tekton** (builder) — same root as English "architect".
Use **ser** without an article: **Él es arquitecto** (He is an architect).
Related word: **la arquitectura** (architecture).
cards.englishPhrase: He is an architect.
cards.phrase: Él es arquitecto.

cards.grammarNote:
Gender forms: **el abogado** / **la abogada**.
From Latin **advocatus** (one called to help) — same root as English "advocate".
Notice the example: **Mi hermana es abogada** — the profession agrees in gender with the subject (**hermana** → **abogada**).
Related: **el derecho** (law/right), **el bufete** (law firm).
cards.englishPhrase: My sister is a lawyer.
cards.phrase: Mi hermana es abogada.

cards.grammarNote:
**El salario** = salary — from Latin **salarium** (allowance to buy salt, **sal**), hence the English word "salary".
Also common: **el sueldo** (wage/pay — more colloquial than **salario**).
**¿Cuál es el salario?** — use **cuál** (which/what) before **es** when asking about identity/value (not **qué**).
**Cuál vs. qué**: **¿Cuál es tu nombre?** (What is your name? — selection from a set) vs. **¿Qué es el amor?** (What is love? — definition).
cards.englishPhrase: What is the salary?
cards.phrase: ¿Cuál es el salario?

cards.grammarNote:
**El horario** = schedule/timetable — from **hora** (hour) + **-ario** (a suffix for things related to something).
**Flexible** is an invariable adjective: **mi horario es flexible** / **mis horarios son flexibles** — same form for masculine/feminine.
**Mi horario es flexible** uses **ser** because schedule type is an inherent characteristic.
Related: **el turno** (shift/turn), **jornada completa** (full-time), **media jornada** (part-time), **hora punta** (rush hour).
cards.englishPhrase: My schedule is flexible.
cards.phrase: Mi horario es flexible.

cards.grammarNote:
**Vacaciones** is almost always used in the plural in Spanish — even for a single trip: **voy de vacaciones** (not *voy de vacación*).
**Ir de vacaciones** = to go on vacation — note **de**, not *en*: **voy de vacaciones** (I'm going on vacation).
**La semana próxima** = next week — **próximo** (next) follows the noun for time: **el mes próximo**, **el año próximo**. Alternatively, **próxima semana** or **la semana que viene** (the week that comes) are also common.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going on vacation next week.
cards.phrase: Voy de vacaciones la semana próxima.

cards.grammarNote:
**El descanso** = break/rest — from **descansar** (to rest).
**Tomar un descanso** = to take a break — **tomar** (literally "to take/drink") is used in many fixed expressions: **tomar un café** (to have a coffee), **tomar asiento** (to take a seat), **tomar una decisión** (to make a decision).
**Tomemos** is the nosotros imperative (let's take): formed from the subjunctive **tomemos**.
Related: **descansar** (to rest), **el recreo** (school recess/break), **la pausa** (pause).
cards.englishPhrase: Let's take a break.
cards.phrase: Tomemos un descanso.

cards.grammarNote:
**La oficina** = office (the room/workplace).
From Latin **officina** (workshop, place of work) — same root as English "office".
**Trabajo en una oficina** — **en** for location (in/at): **en casa** (at home), **en el hospital** (at the hospital).
Related: **el despacho** (personal office/study — Spain), **la empresa** (company/firm), **el edificio de oficinas** (office building).
cards.englishPhrase: I work in an office.
cards.phrase: Trabajo en una oficina.

cards.grammarNote:
**El compañero / la compañera** = companion/colleague — from Latin **companio** (one who shares bread: **com-** together + **panis** bread).
**Compañero de trabajo** = work colleague — **de** specifies the context: **compañero de clase** (classmate), **compañero de piso** (roommate).
**Son simpáticos** uses **ser** for personality: **simpático/a** = friendly/pleasant (a permanent trait).
Note the plural adjective agreement: **compañeros** (m.pl.) → **simpáticos** (m.pl.).
cards.englishPhrase: My coworkers are friendly.
cards.phrase: Mis compañeros de trabajo son simpáticos.

cards.grammarNote:
**El cliente / la cliente** — shared-gender noun (the article changes, the word stays the same).
Also acceptable: **la clienta** (feminine form, less common but used in Spain).
**El cliente está contento** — **estar** for current emotional state (not **ser**): **está contento** = is happy right now.
Compare: **ser contento** is not used; for happiness as a state, always use **estar**.
Related: **la clientela** (clientele/customer base), **atender a un cliente** (to serve a customer).
cards.englishPhrase: The client is happy.
cards.phrase: El cliente está contento.

cards.grammarNote:
**El equipo** = team (work context) or equipment (sports/technical context) — context clarifies.
**Trabajo en un equipo genial** — **en** for membership: **trabajar en un equipo** (to work on a team), **jugar en un equipo** (to play on a team).
**Genial** = great/awesome (colloquial) — literally "genial/genius-like". An invariable adjective: **un equipo genial** / **una idea genial**.
Note: in team sports, Spanish treats the team as a collective singular: **el equipo juega** (the team plays).
cards.englishPhrase: I work in a great team.
cards.phrase: Trabajo en un equipo genial.

cards.grammarNote:
**El proyecto** = project — from Latin **projectum** (thrown forward): **pro-** (forward) + **jacere** (to throw). Same root as English "project".
**El proyecto está casi terminado** — **estar** + past participle describes a resulting state: **está terminado** (is finished/completed), **está abierto** (is open), **está cerrado** (is closed).
**Terminado** is the past participle of **terminar**, used here as an adjective agreeing with **proyecto** (masculine).
**Casi** = almost/nearly — an adverb, doesn't change form.
cards.englishPhrase: The project is almost finished.
cards.phrase: El proyecto está casi terminado.

cards.grammarNote:
**La reunión** = meeting — from **reunir** (to gather/unite): **re-** (again) + **unir** (to unite).
**Tenemos una reunión a las diez** — **tener** is used for scheduled events.
**A las diez** = at ten (o'clock) — plural **las** because it's more than one: **a la una** (at one), **a las dos** (at two), **a las diez** (at ten).
Related: **reunirse** (reflexive: to meet/gather), **convocar una reunión** (to call a meeting).
cards.englishPhrase: We have a meeting at ten.
cards.phrase: Tenemos una reunión a las diez.

cards.grammarNote:
**El tiempo libre** = free time — **libre** (free/unoccupied) as opposed to **ocupado** (busy).
**¿Qué haces en tu tiempo libre?** — **haces** is the tú form of **hacer**: **hago, haces, hace, hacemos...**
Note: **¿Qué haces?** (What do you do?) vs. **¿Qué estás haciendo?** (What are you doing right now?).
**Tiempo** has two meanings: **time** (el tiempo libre) and **weather** (¿Qué tiempo hace? — What's the weather like?). Context always clarifies.
cards.englishPhrase: What do you do in your free time?
cards.phrase: ¿Qué haces en tu tiempo libre?

cards.grammarNote:
**Trabajar** is a regular -ar verb: **trabajo, trabajas, trabaja, trabajamos, trabajáis, trabajan**.
Preposition choices: **trabajar en** + place (**trabajo en un hospital** — I work in a hospital), **trabajar como** + profession (**trabajo como enfermera** — I work as a nurse), **trabajar de** + profession (also common: **trabajo de cocinero**).
**Dedicarse a** = to devote oneself to / to work as: **Se dedica a la medicina** (She devotes herself to medicine).
cards.englishPhrase: I work in a hospital.
cards.phrase: Trabajo en un hospital.

cards.grammarNote:
**Me gusta leer** — with **gustar**, use the infinitive for activities: **Me gusta leer, nadar, cocinar**.
For multiple activities, **gustan** is NOT used — keep **gusta** with a list of infinitives: **Me gusta leer y cocinar**.
**Leer** has a spelling change in the gerund: **leyendo** (not *leiendo*) — the unstressed **i** between vowels becomes **y**.
Same pattern: **creer → creyendo**, **caer → cayendo**.
cards.englishPhrase: I like reading.
cards.phrase: Me gusta leer.

cards.grammarNote:
**A ella le gusta escribir** — the **a + pronoun** construction clarifies who likes something, since **le** alone is ambiguous (could be he/she/you formal).
**Escribir** vs. **escribir a mano** (to write by hand) vs. **teclear** (to type).
Related nouns: **la escritura** (writing/script), **el escritor / la escritora** (writer), **el cuento** (short story).
cards.englishPhrase: She likes writing stories.
cards.phrase: A ella le gusta escribir cuentos.

cards.grammarNote:
**A él le encanta pintar** — **encantar** is a stronger form of **gustar** (to love, to adore).
Both **gustar** and **encantar** are "reverse" verbs: the thing enjoyed is the grammatical subject.
**Pintar** (to paint) → **el pintor / la pintora** (painter), **la pintura** (painting/paint), **el cuadro** (painting/picture).
Note: **pintar** covers both painting a wall and creating art — context distinguishes them.
cards.englishPhrase: He loves painting.
cards.phrase: A él le encanta pintar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Dibujar** = to draw (art/sketching). Not to be confused with **dibujos animados** (cartoons/animated drawings).
**Me gusta dibujar** — infinitive after **gustar** for activities.
Related nouns: **el dibujo** (drawing/sketch), **el dibujante / la dibujante** (illustrator/draughtsperson).
Compare: **pintar** (to paint with color), **dibujar** (to draw with lines/pencil).
cards.englishPhrase: I like drawing.
cards.phrase: Me gusta dibujar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Escuchar música** = to listen to music — **escuchar** already means "to listen to", so no preposition is needed (unlike English).
Don't confuse **escuchar** (to listen to, attentively) with **oír** (to hear, passively): **Oigo música** (I hear music in the background) vs. **Escucho música** (I'm actively listening to music).
**Todos los días** = every day — note **todos** (all, masculine plural) agrees with **días**.
cards.englishPhrase: I listen to music every day.
cards.phrase: Escucho música todos los días.

cards.grammarNote:
**Cantar** = to sing. The person who sings is **el cantante / la cantante** (singer) — a shared-gender noun ending in **-ante**.
**A ella le encanta cantar** — **encantar** (to love/adore) works just like **gustar** but is stronger.
Related: **la canción** (song), **el coro** (choir/chorus), **afinar** (to tune/to sing in tune).
cards.englishPhrase: She loves singing.
cards.phrase: A ella le encanta cantar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Tocar** is the correct verb for playing an instrument — never **jugar**.
**Toco la guitarra** · **toca el piano** · **tocamos el violín**
Use **jugar** for sports and games: **jugar al fútbol**, **jugar ajedrez**.
Instruments take the definite article: **toco la guitarra** (not *toco guitarra*).
Related: **el instrumento** (instrument), **la guitarra acústica / eléctrica** (acoustic / electric guitar).
cards.englishPhrase: I play the guitar.
cards.phrase: Toco la guitarra.

cards.grammarNote:
**Nos encanta bailar** — **nos** is the indirect object pronoun for "us".
**Encantar** conjugates to agree with the grammatical subject (what is loved), not the person: **nos encanta** (one thing) vs. **nos encantan** (multiple things).
Related: **el baile** (dance/dancing), **la bailarina / el bailarín** (ballet dancer), **el salón de baile** (ballroom).
**Bailar** is also used in expressions: **bailar salsa/tango/flamenco**.
cards.englishPhrase: We love dancing.
cards.phrase: Nos encanta bailar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Cocinar** (to cook) vs. **cocina** (kitchen / cuisine) — same root, different form.
**Me gusta cocinar** — infinitive after **gustar** for activities.
For professional cooking, use **el cocinero / la cocinera** (cook) or **el/la chef**.
**Practicar** is used for hobbies/sports in general, but **cocinar** is the direct verb: say **me gusta cocinar**, not *practico la cocina* (unnatural).
cards.englishPhrase: I enjoy cooking.
cards.phrase: Me gusta cocinar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Hacer senderismo** = to go hiking — many outdoor activities in Spanish use **hacer**: **hacer senderismo**, **hacer yoga**, **hacer ejercicio**, **hacer surf**.
Alternatively: **ir de senderismo** (to go hiking).
**Senderismo** comes from **sendero** (path/trail).
Related: **la montaña** (mountain), **el monte** (hill/mountain/wilderness), **la ruta** (route/trail).
cards.englishPhrase: I like hiking in the mountains.
cards.phrase: Me gusta hacer senderismo en la montaña.

cards.grammarNote:
**Correr** = to run (a regular -er verb).
**Corro** (I run), **corres**, **corre**, **corremos**, **corréis**, **corren**.
**Todas las mañanas** = every morning — **todas** (all, feminine plural) agrees with **mañanas**.
Compare: **correr** (to run in general) vs. **trotar** (to jog at a light pace) vs. **hacer running** (to go for a run, borrowed term).
cards.englishPhrase: I run every morning.
cards.phrase: Corro todas las mañanas.

cards.grammarNote:
**Nadar** = to swim (a regular -ar verb).
**Me gusta nadar** — infinitive after **gustar** for activities.
For "to go swimming" use **ir a nadar** or **ir a la piscina** (to go to the pool).
Related: **la piscina** (pool), **el mar** (sea), **la playa** (beach), **el nadador / la nadadora** (swimmer).
**Practicar la natación** (to practice swimming) is also used in more formal contexts.
cards.englishPhrase: I like swimming.
cards.phrase: Me gusta nadar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Andar en bicicleta** = to ride a bike — literally "to walk/go by bicycle".
Also common: **montar en bicicleta** (especially in Spain) or **ir en bici** (informal).
**Andar** here means "to go/travel" rather than "to walk on foot".
**Los fines de semana** = on weekends — **el fin de semana** (the weekend), plural **los fines de semana**.
cards.englishPhrase: I go biking on weekends.
cards.phrase: Ando en bicicleta los fines de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Me encanta viajar** — **encantar** + infinitive = to love doing something.
**Viajar** is a regular -ar verb: **viajo, viajas, viaja, viajamos, viajáis, viajan**.
Related: **el viaje** (trip/journey), **el viajero / la viajera** (traveler), **viajar al extranjero** (to travel abroad).
**Ir de viaje** (to go on a trip) is a common alternative expression.
cards.englishPhrase: I love traveling.
cards.phrase: Me encanta viajar.

cards.grammarNote:
Stem-changing verb: **jugar** (u→ue): **juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan**.
With video games, **jugar** is used directly or with **a**: **juega videojuegos** or **juega a los videojuegos**.
Compare with sports: **jugar al fútbol** (requires **al**) — with videojuegos, the **a** is often dropped in informal speech.
**Por la noche** = at night/in the evening — compare: **por la mañana** (in the morning), **por la tarde** (in the afternoon).
cards.englishPhrase: He plays video games at night.
cards.phrase: Él juega videojuegos por la noche.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ver** = to watch/see (an irregular yo form: **veo**): **veo, ves, ve, vemos, veis, ven**.
**Me gusta ver películas** — infinitive after **gustar**.
Distinction: **ver la tele/televisión** (to watch TV), **ver una película** (to watch a movie), **ver una serie** (to watch a series/show).
**Películas** (movies) from **película** — originally "film strip" (related to **piel**, skin/film).
cards.englishPhrase: I like watching movies.
cards.phrase: Me gusta ver películas.

cards.grammarNote:
**Escuchar** = to listen to — the "to" is built in, no extra preposition needed.
**A ella le gusta escuchar música** — the **a ella** clarifies who likes it, because **le** alone is ambiguous.
Distinction: **escuchar** (active, attentive listening) vs. **oír** (passive hearing).
Related: **el oyente** (listener), **la canción** (song), **el álbum** (album).
cards.englishPhrase: She likes listening to music.
cards.phrase: A ella le gusta escuchar música.

cards.grammarNote:
**Hacer ejercicio** = to exercise — **hacer** is the go-to verb for physical activities.
**Voy al gimnasio** — **al** is the mandatory contraction of **a + el**: never *a el gimnasio*.
**Para + infinitive** expresses purpose: **voy al gimnasio para hacer ejercicio** (I go to the gym in order to exercise).
Related: **el gimnasio** (gym), **entrenarse** (to train/work out), **el entrenador / la entrenadora** (trainer).
cards.englishPhrase: I go to the gym for exercise.
cards.phrase: Voy al gimnasio para hacer ejercicio.

cards.grammarNote:
**Al aire libre** = outdoors / in the open air — a fixed expression: **al** (a + el) + **aire** (air) + **libre** (free/open).
**Al** is the mandatory contraction of **a + el**: **al parque**, **al trabajo**, **al aire libre**.
**Trabajar al aire libre** — many professions involve outdoor work: **jardinero, agricultor, guía turístico, bombero**.
Related: **afuera** (outside), **en el exterior** (on the outside/outdoors — more formal).
cards.englishPhrase: She works outdoors.
cards.phrase: Ella trabaja al aire libre.

cards.grammarNote:
**Creativo** is a quality adjective that changes for gender and number: **creativo** (m.sg.) / **creativa** (f.sg.) / **creativos** (m.pl.) / **creativas** (f.pl.).
Note the example: **Ella es muy creativa** — the adjective agrees with **ella** (feminine), so **creativa**.
Use **ser** for permanent character traits: **es creativa** (she is creative by nature).
Related: **la creatividad** (creativity), **crear** (to create), **la creación** (creation).
cards.englishPhrase: She is very creative.
cards.phrase: Ella es muy creativa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Interesante** is an invariable adjective — it does NOT change for gender: **un trabajo interesante** / **una idea interesante** (same form).
Adjectives ending in **-e** or consonants are typically invariable for gender (they still change for number: **interesantes**).
Use **ser** for inherent qualities: **Mi trabajo es interesante** (permanent characteristic).
Related: **interesar** (to interest) — works like **gustar**: **Me interesa la música** (Music interests me).
cards.englishPhrase: My job is interesting.
cards.phrase: Mi trabajo es interesante.

cards.grammarNote:
**Aburrido** changes for gender and number: **aburrido** (m.sg.) / **aburrida** (f.sg.) / **aburridos / aburridas** (plural).
Note: **La reunión fue aburrida** — the adjective agrees with **la reunión** (feminine).
**Fue** is the preterite of both **ser** and **ir** — they share the same preterite forms: **fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron**. Context clarifies meaning.
**Ser vs. estar with aburrido**: **ser aburrido** = to be a boring (person/thing by nature); **estar aburrido** = to feel bored (current state).
cards.englishPhrase: The meeting was boring.
cards.phrase: La reunión fue aburrida.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ganar** = to earn / to win / to gain (a regular -ar verb).
Context determines meaning: **ganar dinero** (to earn money), **ganar un partido** (to win a game), **ganar experiencia** (to gain experience).
**Buen** vs. **bueno**: the adjective **bueno** shortens to **buen** before a masculine singular noun: **buen salario**, **buen trabajo**, **buen hombre**.
**Salario** comes from Latin **salarium** — the allowance given to Roman soldiers to buy salt (**sal**).
cards.englishPhrase: He earns a good salary.
cards.phrase: Él gana un buen salario.

cards.grammarNote:
**Jubilarse** is a reflexive verb — the reflexive pronoun changes with each subject: **me jubilo, te jubilas, se jubila, nos jubilamos...**
**Se jubiló** = she retired — preterite (past) tense, with the accent on the final syllable marking the preterite.
**El año pasado** = last year — **pasado** (past/last) follows the noun: **la semana pasada**, **el mes pasado**.
From **júbilo** (joy) — compare English "jubilee".
cards.englishPhrase: She retired last year.
cards.phrase: Ella se jubiló el año pasado.

cards.grammarNote:
**Tener** = to have (an irregular -er verb): **tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen**.
Note the irregular yo form: **tengo** (not *teno*).
**Buen** shortens before masculine singular nouns: **buen trabajo**, **buen salario** (but **buena idea** with feminine nouns).
**Tener** vs. **haber**: **tener** = to have/possess; **hay** (from haber) = there is/there are.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a good job.
cards.phrase: Tengo un buen trabajo.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estar desempleado** — use **estar** (not **ser**) for states that can change: unemployment is temporary.
Compare: **Soy médico** (I am a doctor — identity) vs. **Estoy desempleado** (I am unemployed — current state).
**Desempleado** = unemployed — from **des-** (un-) + **empleado** (employed, from **emplear**, to employ).
Alternatives: **estar en paro** (Spain, colloquial), **estar sin trabajo** (to be without work).
cards.englishPhrase: He is currently unemployed.
cards.phrase: Él está desempleado actualmente.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estudiar** = to study (a regular -ar verb): **estudio, estudias, estudia, estudiamos, estudiáis, estudian**.
**Todos los días** = every day — **todos** (all, masculine plural) agrees with **días** (days).
Compare **estudiar** (to study a subject) vs. **aprender** (to learn/acquire knowledge): **Estudio medicina** (I study medicine) vs. **Aprendo español** (I'm learning Spanish).
cards.englishPhrase: I study every day.
cards.phrase: Estudio todos los días.

cards.grammarNote:
**Aprender** = to learn (a regular -er verb): **aprendo, aprendes, aprende, aprendemos, aprendéis, aprenden**.
**Estoy aprendiendo** = I am learning — present progressive: **estar** + gerund (**aprendiendo**).
In Spanish, the simple present often replaces the progressive for ongoing situations: **aprendo español** is equally natural.
Related: **el aprendizaje** (learning/apprenticeship), **aprender de memoria** (to memorize/learn by heart).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm learning Spanish.
cards.phrase: Estoy aprendiendo español.

cards.grammarNote:
**Practicar** = to practice (a sport, hobby, or skill) — use this for non-game activities.
Don't use **jugar** for non-competitive activities: say **practico yoga**, **practico natación**, **practico senderismo**.
For sports framed as competition or play, **jugar** is also correct: **juego al tenis** (I play tennis) or **practico el tenis**.
**Practico** (I practice) — note the spelling change: **c → qu** before **e/i**: **practiqué** (I practiced, preterite).
cards.englishPhrase: I practice every day.
cards.phrase: Practico todos los días.

cards.grammarNote:
**Enseñar** = to teach / to show (a regular -ar verb).
Note that **enseñar** means both "to teach" and "to show": **Me enseña la foto** (She shows me the photo) vs. **Enseña español** (She teaches Spanish).
The person who teaches: **el profesor / la profesora** (teacher/professor) — gender forms differ.
Related: **la enseñanza** (teaching/education), **el colegio** (school), **dar clases** (to give classes/teach).
cards.englishPhrase: She teaches Spanish.
cards.phrase: Ella enseña español.

cards.grammarNote:
**Construir** belongs to a group of -uir verbs that insert a **y** before vowel endings: **construyo, construyes, construye, construimos, construís, construyen**.
The gerund: **construyendo** (building) — the **y** appears there too.
**Están construyendo** = they are building — present progressive.
Related: **la construcción** (construction), **el constructor / la constructora** (builder), **el edificio** (building).
cards.englishPhrase: They are building a new school.
cards.phrase: Están construyendo una nueva escuela.

cards.grammarNote:
**Arreglar** = to fix / to arrange / to tidy (a regular -ar verb).
Context determines the meaning: **arreglar el coche** (to fix the car), **arreglar la habitación** (to tidy the room), **arreglarse** (to get ready/dressed up — reflexive).
**¿Puedes arreglar esto?** — **poder** (can/to be able to) is a stem-changing verb (o→ue): **puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden**.
**Esto** = this (neuter demonstrative, used when the noun is unspecified).
cards.englishPhrase: Can you fix this?
cards.phrase: ¿Puedes arreglar esto?

cards.grammarNote:
**Hacer** = to make / to do — one of the most versatile and irregular verbs in Spanish.
Irregular yo form: **hago** (not *haco*).
Full present: **hago, haces, hace, hacemos, hacéis, hacen**.
**Hacer** is used for many activities: **hacer ejercicio** (to exercise), **hacer yoga**, **hacer senderismo**, **hacer la tarea** (to do homework), **hacer una llamada** (to make a call).
**Hago café** — note no article needed: **hacer café**, **hacer ejercicio** (activity as a mass/abstract noun).
cards.englishPhrase: I make coffee every morning.
cards.phrase: Hago café todas las mañanas.

cards.grammarNote:
**Diseñar** = to design (a regular -ar verb).
The person who designs: **el diseñador / la diseñadora** (designer).
**Páginas web** = websites — literally "web pages". Also: **sitios web** (websites) or just **webs** (colloquial).
Related fields: **el diseño gráfico** (graphic design), **el diseño web** (web design), **el diseño industrial** (industrial design).
Compare with **dibujar** (to draw): **diseñar** implies intentional planning/creation for a purpose.
cards.englishPhrase: He designs websites.
cards.phrase: Él diseña páginas web.

cards.grammarNote:
**Vender** = to sell (a regular -er verb): **vendo, vendes, vende, vendemos, vendéis, venden**.
The person who sells: **el vendedor / la vendedora** (salesperson/seller).
Related: **la venta** (sale), **en venta** (for sale), **comprar** (to buy — the opposite).
Note: **coches** (cars) is the Spain variant; in Latin America you'll hear **carros** or **autos** instead.
cards.englishPhrase: He sells cars.
cards.phrase: Él vende coches.

cards.grammarNote:
**Comprar** = to buy (a regular -ar verb): **compro, compras, compra, compramos, compráis, compran**.
**Necesito comprar** — **necesitar + infinitive** = to need to do something: **necesito estudiar** (I need to study).
**Computadora** = computer (Latin America); in Spain: **el ordenador**. Both are correct.
Related: **la tienda** (store), **el precio** (price), **la oferta** (sale/offer), **las compras** (shopping).
cards.englishPhrase: I need to buy a new computer.
cards.phrase: Necesito comprar una nueva computadora.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ayudar** = to help (a regular -ar verb).
**¿Puedo ayudarte?** — **ayudarte** is an infinitive with a clitic pronoun attached: **ayudar** + **te** (you).
This is called an "attached pronoun" on an infinitive. Alternatively: **¿Te puedo ayudar?** (same meaning, pronoun before the conjugated verb).
**Puedo** = I can — from **poder** (o→ue stem-changer): **puedo, puedes, puede...**
**Ayudar a** + person: **Te ayudo a encontrarlo** (I'll help you find it).
cards.englishPhrase: Can I help you?
cards.phrase: ¿Puedo ayudarte?

cards.grammarNote:
**Dirigir** = to manage / to direct / to lead (an -ir verb).
Irregular yo form: **dirijo** (not *dirigo*) — the **g** changes to **j** before **o** to preserve the soft sound.
Full present: **dirijo, diriges, dirige, dirigimos, dirigís, dirigen**.
Related: **el director / la directora** (director/manager), **la dirección** (management/direction/address).
Alternatives for "to manage": **gestionar** (to manage/administer), **administrar** (to administer).
cards.englishPhrase: She manages the team.
cards.phrase: Ella dirige el equipo.

cards.grammarNote:
**Reunirse** = to meet/gather (a reflexive verb).
Reflexive pronouns: **me reúno, te reúnes, se reúne, nos reunimos, os reunís, se reúnen**.
Note the accent: **reúno, reúnes, reúne, reúnen** — the stress falls on the **ú** in most forms (but NOT in nosotros/vosotros).
**Nos reunimos** = we meet — note no accent here (stress on **ni** is regular).
**Cada lunes** = every Monday — **cada** (each/every) + singular: **cada día**, **cada semana**, **cada mes**.
cards.englishPhrase: We meet every Monday.
cards.phrase: Nos reunimos cada lunes.

cards.grammarNote:
**Empezar** is a stem-changing verb (e→ie): **empiezo, empiezas, empieza, empezamos, empezáis, empiezan**.
Note: no stem change in **nosotros/vosotros** forms.
**Empezar a + infinitive** = to start doing something: **empiezo a trabajar** (I start working).
Note also the spelling change: **z → c** before **e** in preterite: **empecé** (I started).
Synonym: **comenzar** (identical conjugation pattern — also e→ie).
cards.englishPhrase: I start work at eight.
cards.phrase: Empiezo a trabajar a las ocho.

cards.grammarNote:
**Terminar** = to finish / to end (a regular -ar verb).
**Terminar de + infinitive** = to finish doing something: **termino de trabajar** (I finish working), **terminé de comer** (I finished eating).
Compare: **terminar** (to finish) vs. **empezar** (to start) — natural opposites.
**A las cinco** = at five (o'clock) — telling time: **a la una** (at one), **a las dos/tres...** (at two/three...).
cards.englishPhrase: I finish work at five.
cards.phrase: Termino de trabajar a las cinco.

cards.grammarNote:
**gustar** + infinitive = to like doing something
**Me gusta leer** (I like reading) · **A ella le gusta cantar** (She likes singing)
For clarity with third-person subjects, add **a** + person: **A mi padre le gusta pescar**
**gustar** agrees with what is liked, not the person doing the liking
cards.englishPhrase: I like reading. She likes singing.
cards.phrase: Me gusta leer. A ella le gusta cantar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Relajarse** is a reflexive verb: **me relajo, te relajas, se relaja, nos relajamos...**
**Me relajo** = I relax — the reflexive **me** shows the action reflects back on the subject.
Reflexive verbs for mental/physical states are very common in Spanish: **relajarse** (to relax), **distraerse** (to get distracted), **concentrarse** (to focus), **aburrirse** (to get bored).
**Los fines de semana** = on weekends — **los** + time noun expresses recurrence.
cards.englishPhrase: I relax on weekends.
cards.phrase: Me relajo los fines de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estresante** is another invariable adjective (ending in **-ante**): **un trabajo estresante** / **una situación estresante** — same form for masculine and feminine.
Borrowed from English "stress" → **estrés** (noun, masculine: **el estrés**) → **estresante** (adjective) → **estresarse** (reflexive verb: to get stressed).
Use **ser** for a job's inherent quality: **Mi trabajo es estresante**.
Contrast with **estar estresado/a** (to feel stressed right now — a temporary state).
cards.englishPhrase: My job is stressful.
cards.phrase: Mi trabajo es estresante.

cards.grammarNote:
Adverb form: **felizmente** (happily) — add **-mente** to the feminine adjective
**feliz** has no gender change: feliz + mente → **felizmente** · **Ella sonrió felizmente.**
cards.englishPhrase: I'm very happy today.
cards.phrase: Estoy muy feliz hoy.

cards.grammarNote: Adverb form: **tristemente** (sadly) — **triste** has no gender change: triste + mente → **tristemente** · **Habló tristemente.**
cards.englishPhrase: Why are you sad?
cards.phrase: ¿Por qué estás triste?

cards.grammarNote:
**amor** comes from Latin **amor** (love, desire) — the same root as English *amorous*.
Verb forms: **amar** (to love deeply), **querer** (to love/want — more everyday).
**Te quiero** (I love you — common between family/friends) vs **Te amo** (I love you — more intense/romantic).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel a lot of love for my family.
cards.phrase: Siento mucho amor por mi familia.

cards.grammarNote:
**enojo** = anger, annoyance — the most common everyday word across Latin America.
**enfado** is more common in Spain.
**ira** = wrath/rage — strong and formal, from Latin. You'd use it in writing or when describing intense anger.
**Me dio enojo** = it made me angry (lit. "it gave me anger") — **dar** is commonly used this way: **me da risa** (it makes me laugh), **me da miedo** (it scares me).
cards.englishPhrase: It made me angry when they lied to me.
cards.phrase: Me dio enojo cuando me mintieron.

cards.grammarNote:
**tener miedo** = to be afraid (literally *to have fear*) — Spanish uses **tener** + noun for many states.
**tener miedo de/a + infinitive**: **tengo miedo de caer** (I'm afraid of falling).
Also: **dar miedo** = to frighten — **me da miedo** (it frightens me / it scares me).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm afraid of the dark.
cards.phrase: Tengo miedo de la oscuridad.

cards.grammarNote:
**esperanza** (hope) is a noun; the verb is **esperar** (to hope, to wait, to expect).
Note the suffix **-anza** forming abstract nouns: **confianza** (trust), **enseñanza** (teaching), **esperanza** (hope).
**Espero que + subjunctive**: **espero que todo salga bien** (I hope everything goes well).
cards.englishPhrase: I have hope for the future.
cards.phrase: Tengo esperanza en el futuro.

cards.grammarNote:
**estrés** is a borrowed word from English *stress* — note the accent on the final syllable.
The adjective is **estresado/a** (stressed): **estoy estresado** (I'm stressed) — uses **estar** for the temporary state.
Also: **estresante** (stressful) — **un trabajo estresante** (a stressful job).
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of stress at work.
cards.phrase: Tengo mucho estrés en el trabajo.

cards.grammarNote:
**estado de ánimo** = mood (literally *state of spirit/soul*).
**ánimo** alone means spirit, cheer, courage — **¡Ánimo!** = Cheer up! / Come on!
Also common: **estar de buen humor** (to be in a good mood) and **estar de mal humor** (to be in a bad mood).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm in a good mood today.
cards.phrase: Hoy estoy de buen estado de ánimo.

cards.grammarNote:
**sentimiento** (feeling, emotion) comes from **sentir** (to feel).
The suffix **-miento** forms nouns from verbs: **sentir → sentimiento**, **conocer → conocimiento** (knowledge), **pensar → pensamiento** (thought).
Also related: **sentido** = sense (as in the five senses, or *meaning*).
cards.englishPhrase: That feeling is normal.
cards.phrase: Ese sentimiento es normal.

cards.grammarNote:
**emoción** = emotion, but also *excitement* — context determines the meaning.
The verb **emocionar** = to move emotionally / to excite: **me emociona** (it moves me / it excites me).
Reflexive **emocionarse** = to get emotional: **se emocionó** (he/she got emotional / teared up).
cards.englishPhrase: I couldn't hide my emotion.
cards.phrase: No pude ocultar mi emoción.

cards.grammarNote:
**calma** (noun) = calm, calmness.
Adjective form: **tranquilo/a** or **calmado/a** (calm, relaxed).
Use **estar** for the temporary state: **estoy tranquilo** (I'm calm right now) vs **soy tranquilo** (I'm a calm person by nature).
Also: **mantener la calma** (to keep calm) — a very common phrase.
cards.englishPhrase: Try to maintain your calm.
cards.phrase: Intenta mantener la calma.

cards.grammarNote:
**preocupación** (worry, concern) — noun from **preocupar** (to worry/concern).
The reflexive **preocuparse** = to worry oneself: **me preocupo** (I worry), **no te preocupes** (don't worry).
The suffix **-ción** forms feminine nouns from verbs: **preocupar → preocupación**, **emocionar → emoción**.
cards.englishPhrase: Don't let worry stop you.
cards.phrase: No dejes que la preocupación te detenga.

cards.grammarNote:
**sorpresa** (surprise) — from **sorprender** (to surprise).
**¡Qué sorpresa!** = What a surprise! — the **¡Qué + noun!** structure expresses exclamation.
Adjective: **sorprendido/a** (surprised) — use **estar**: **estoy sorprendido** (I'm surprised).
Also: **me sorprendió** (it surprised me) — verb used like **gustar** with indirect object pronouns.
cards.englishPhrase: What a surprise!
cards.phrase: ¡Qué sorpresa!

cards.grammarNote:
**odio** = hate (noun) — also the yo form of **odiar** (to hate): **yo odio** (I hate).
Note that **odio** as a noun takes a definite article: **el odio es destructivo** (hate is destructive).
Compare: **ira** (wrath/anger — more formal), **rencor** (resentment, grudge), **enojo** (everyday anger).
cards.englishPhrase: Hate is a strong feeling.
cards.phrase: El odio es un sentimiento fuerte.

cards.grammarNote:
**dolor** (pain) — from Latin **dolor**, same root as English *dolorous*.
**tener dolor de + body part**: **tengo dolor de cabeza** (I have a headache), **tengo dolor de estómago** (I have a stomachache).
Verb: **doler** (to hurt/ache) — works like **gustar**: **me duele la cabeza** (my head hurts — lit. the head hurts me).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel pain in my leg.
cards.phrase: Siento dolor en la pierna.

cards.grammarNote:
**energía** (energy) — note the accent on the **í** (énfasis on the third syllable from the end).
**tener energía** = to have energy — using **tener** for states: **tengo mucha energía** (I have a lot of energy).
Adjective: **enérgico/a** (energetic) — use **ser** for a personality trait: **es muy enérgico** (he's very energetic).
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of energy today.
cards.phrase: Hoy tengo mucha energía.

cards.grammarNote:
**sentir** = to feel/perceive something · **sentirse** (reflexive) = to feel a certain way
**Me siento bien** (I feel good) · **Siento dolor** (I feel pain)
cards.englishPhrase: I feel good today.
cards.phrase: Me siento bien hoy.

cards.grammarNote:
**amar** = to love (deeply, often romantic or profound love).
Compare **querer** = to love/want — more versatile and common in everyday speech: **te quiero** (I love you) is used between family and close friends.
**Te amo** is more intense and typically romantic; **te quiero** is warmer and more common day-to-day.
cards.englishPhrase: I love you very much.
cards.phrase: Te amo mucho.

cards.grammarNote:
**odiar** = to hate — a regular -ar verb: **odio, odias, odia, odiamos, odiáis, odian**.
**odiar + infinitive** = to hate doing something: **odio esperar** (I hate waiting), **odia llegar tarde** (he hates being late).
Less intense alternatives: **no soportar** (can't stand), **detestar** (to detest).
cards.englishPhrase: I hate waiting.
cards.phrase: Odio esperar.

cards.grammarNote:
**gustar** works opposite to English — the subject is what is liked, not the person.
**Me gusta la música** = Music pleases me (I like music).
Indirect object pronouns: **me** (to me), **te** (to you), **le** (to him/her), **nos** (to us), **les** (to them).
**Me gustan** (plural) vs **me gusta** (singular): **me gustan los libros** (I like books).
cards.englishPhrase: I like music.
cards.phrase: Me gusta la música.

cards.grammarNote:
**disfrutar** = to enjoy — can take **de** or a direct object: **disfrutar de la vida** or **disfrutar la vida**.
Both are correct; **disfrutar de** is slightly more formal.
Also reflexive: **disfrutarse** is used in some Latin American countries — **¡disfrútalo!** (enjoy it!).
cards.englishPhrase: I enjoy the weekend.
cards.phrase: Disfruto el fin de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**tener miedo** = to be afraid / to be scared (lit. "to have fear") — the most natural everyday expression.
**Me da miedo** = it scares me (lit. "it gives me fear") — very common: **me da miedo volar** (flying scares me).
**temer** = to fear — a regular -er verb but formal/literary. You'd see it in writing more than speech.
**miedoso/a** = scaredy-cat / easily scared (adjective).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm afraid of spiders.
cards.phrase: Tengo miedo de las arañas.

cards.grammarNote:
**esperar** has three meanings: to hope, to wait, and to expect.
**esperar que + subjunctive** = to hope that: **espero que todo salga bien** (I hope everything goes well).
**esperar a + infinitive** = to wait to do something: **espero a ver** (I'll wait and see).
Context clarifies which meaning is intended — often all three blend together.
cards.englishPhrase: I hope everything goes well.
cards.phrase: Espero que todo salga bien.

cards.grammarNote:
**preocuparse** is a reflexive verb — to worry oneself.
Full conjugation: **me preocupo, te preocupas, se preocupa, nos preocupamos**.
**No te preocupes** = Don't worry — the **te** is the reflexive pronoun (tú form).
Non-reflexive **preocupar** = to worry someone else: **me preocupa** (it worries me / I'm worried about it).
cards.englishPhrase: Don't worry about it.
cards.phrase: No te preocupes por eso.

cards.grammarNote:
**paz** (peace) — from Latin **pax** (same root as English *pacify*, *pacific*).
Note the plural: **paces** (though rarely used). The phrase **hacer las paces** = to make peace / to make up.
**tranquilidad** (quiet, tranquility) is a close synonym — **necesito paz y tranquilidad** (I need peace and quiet).
cards.englishPhrase: I need peace and quiet.
cards.phrase: Necesito paz y tranquilidad.

cards.grammarNote: **celos** is typically plural · **tener celos** = to be jealous · **envidia** = envy (wanting what someone else has)
cards.englishPhrase: She feels jealous.
cards.phrase: Ella siente celos.

cards.grammarNote:
**molestar** = to bother, to annoy — works like **gustar**: the annoying thing is the subject.
**Ese ruido me molesta** = That noise bothers me (lit. that noise molests/disturbs me).
Reflexive **molestarse** = to be bothered / to take the trouble: **no te molestes** (don't bother).
Note: **molestar** is not as strong as English *molest* — it simply means to disturb or annoy.
cards.englishPhrase: That noise annoys me.
cards.phrase: Ese ruido me molesta.

cards.grammarNote:
**enojar** = to anger (someone else) — transitive: **ese comentario me enojó** (that comment angered me).
Reflexive **enojarse** = to get angry: **me enojé** (I got angry), **se enoja fácilmente** (he gets angry easily).
**ponerse enojado/a** = to become angry — **se puso enojada** (she became angry).
Note: **enojado** uses **estar** — **estoy enojado** (I'm angry right now).
cards.englishPhrase: That comment angered me.
cards.phrase: Ese comentario me enojó.

cards.grammarNote:
**sonreír** = to smile — a compound of **son-** (sound/tone) + **reír** (to laugh).
**sonreír** is an irregular e→i stem-changing verb: **sonrío, sonríes, sonríe, sonreímos, sonreís, sonríen**.
Noun: **la sonrisa** (the smile) — **tiene una sonrisa hermosa** (she has a beautiful smile).
Note the written accent on **sonríe** to separate the two vowels.
cards.englishPhrase: She always smiles.
cards.phrase: Ella siempre sonríe.

cards.grammarNote:
**reír** = to laugh — irregular e→i stem-changing verb: **río, ríes, ríe, reímos, reís, ríen**.
Reflexive **reírse** is also common and essentially interchangeable: **nos reímos** (we laughed).
**reírse de** = to laugh at: **se ríen de mí** (they're laughing at me).
Noun: **la risa** (the laugh, laughter) — **me dio risa** (it made me laugh).
cards.englishPhrase: We laughed a lot.
cards.phrase: Nos reímos mucho.

cards.grammarNote:
**llorar** = to cry — a regular -ar verb: **lloro, lloras, llora, lloramos, lloráis, lloran**.
The present progressive **está llorando** (is crying) uses **estar** + gerund (-ando/-iendo).
**hacerse llorar** = to make someone cry: **me hizo llorar** (it made me cry).
Note: **llover** (to rain) sounds similar but is unrelated — **llueve** (it's raining).
cards.englishPhrase: The baby is crying.
cards.phrase: El bebé está llorando.

cards.grammarNote:
**gritar** = to shout, to scream — a regular -ar verb.
**No grites** = Don't shout — negative tú command: use the present subjunctive (**grites**).
Noun: **el grito** (the shout, scream) — **un grito de alegría** (a cry of joy), **a voces / a gritos** (shouting, at the top of one's voice).
Also: **dar un grito** = to let out a shout.
cards.englishPhrase: Don't shout, please.
cards.phrase: No grites, por favor.

cards.grammarNote:
**relajarse** is a reflexive verb — to relax (oneself).
**Relájate** = Relax! — affirmative tú command of the reflexive: drop **-s** from **te relajas**, then attach **-te**: **relájate** (note the accent to preserve stress).
Full conjugation: **me relajo, te relajas, se relaja, nos relajamos**.
Also: **estar relajado/a** = to be relaxed (state) — **estoy muy relajado** (I'm very relaxed).
cards.englishPhrase: Relax, there's no rush.
cards.phrase: Relájate, no hay prisa.

cards.grammarNote: Adverb form: **enojadamente** (angrily) — feminine: enojada + mente → **enojadamente** · **Respondió enojadamente.**
cards.englishPhrase: I'm angry with you.
cards.phrase: Estoy enojado contigo.

cards.grammarNote:
**asustado/a** = scared, frightened — past participle of **asustar** (to frighten) used as an adjective.
Always use **estar**: **estaba asustado** (he was scared) — a temporary emotional state.
Verb: **asustarse** (reflexive) = to get scared: **me asusté** (I got scared), **no te asustes** (don't get scared).
Also: **tener miedo** (to be afraid) and **asustado** often overlap — **tenía miedo** vs **estaba asustado**.
cards.englishPhrase: The child was scared.
cards.phrase: El niño estaba asustado.

cards.grammarNote: Adverb form: **ansiosamente** (anxiously) — feminine: ansiosa + mente → **ansiosamente** · **Esperaba ansiosamente.**
cards.englishPhrase: I'm anxious about the exam.
cards.phrase: Estoy ansioso por el examen.

cards.grammarNote: Adverb form: **nerviosamente** (nervously) — feminine: nerviosa + mente → **nerviosamente** · **Habló nerviosamente.**
cards.englishPhrase: I'm nervous today.
cards.phrase: Estoy nervioso hoy.

cards.grammarNote: Adverb form: **emocionadamente** (excitedly) — feminine: emocionada + mente → **emocionadamente** · **Gritó emocionadamente.**
cards.englishPhrase: I'm excited about the trip.
cards.phrase: Estoy emocionado por el viaje.

cards.grammarNote:
**alegre** (joyful, cheerful) — from Latin **alacer** (lively, brisk), the same root as **alegría** (joy).
The suffix **-ía** forms abstract nouns: **alegre → alegría** (joy), **cortés → cortesía** (courtesy).
Note the use of **estar**: **siempre está alegre** (she's always cheerful) — even with *siempre*, **estar** is used because it describes a perceived/observed state.
**ponerse alegre** = to become cheerful/tipsy — **me pongo alegre con el vino** (wine makes me happy/tipsy).
cards.englishPhrase: She is always cheerful.
cards.phrase: Ella siempre está alegre.

cards.grammarNote: Adverb form: **orgullosamente** (proudly) — feminine: orgullosa + mente → **orgullosamente** · **Sonrió orgullosamente.**
cards.englishPhrase: I'm proud of you.
cards.phrase: Estoy orgulloso de ti.

cards.grammarNote:
**contento/a** = content, happy, pleased — always use **estar**: **estoy contento** (I'm content/pleased).
Do not confuse with **contento** as a noun (rarely used) or **contenido** (content, as in the content of a book).
**sentirse contento** = to feel content: **me siento contento con mi vida** (I feel content with my life).
Related: **satisfecho/a** (satisfied) — **estoy satisfecho** (I'm satisfied).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm content with my life.
cards.phrase: Estoy contento con mi vida.

cards.grammarNote: Adverb form: **tranquilamente** (calmly) — feminine: tranquila + mente → **tranquilamente** · **Respondió tranquilamente.**
cards.englishPhrase: Stay calm, everything is fine.
cards.phrase: Mantente tranquilo, todo está bien.

cards.grammarNote:
**estresado/a** = stressed — past participle of **estresar** used as an adjective.
Always use **estar**: **estoy muy estresado** (I'm very stressed) — a temporary state, not a permanent personality trait.
**ponerse estresado** = to become stressed: **me pongo estresado cuando hay mucho trabajo** (I get stressed when there's a lot of work).
The noun **estrés** is a loanword from English — note the accent on the final syllable.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm very stressed this week.
cards.phrase: Estoy muy estresado esta semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**abrumado/a** = overwhelmed — from **abrumar** (to overwhelm, to weigh down).
**sentirse abrumado** uses the reflexive **sentirse**: **me siento abrumado** (I feel overwhelmed).
Use **estar** for the resulting state: **estoy abrumado** (I'm overwhelmed).
The preposition **por** marks the cause: **abrumado por el trabajo** (overwhelmed by the work).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel overwhelmed by the work.
cards.phrase: Me siento abrumado por el trabajo.

cards.grammarNote:
**energético/a** = energetic — adjective from **energía** (energy).
Use **ser** for a personality trait: **es muy energética** (she's very energetic by nature).
Contrast with **estar lleno/a de energía** (to be full of energy — a current state): **hoy estoy lleno de energía**.
Note gender agreement: **energético** (masculine), **energética** (feminine).
cards.englishPhrase: She is very energetic.
cards.phrase: Ella es muy energética.

cards.grammarNote: Adverb form: **cansadamente** (wearily) — feminine: cansada + mente → **cansadamente** · **Arrastró los pies cansadamente.**
cards.englishPhrase: I'm very tired today.
cards.phrase: Estoy muy cansado hoy.

cards.grammarNote:
**agotado/a** = exhausted, depleted — from **agotar** (to exhaust, to drain, to use up).
Always use **estar**: **estoy agotado** (I'm exhausted) — a temporary physical/emotional state.
**agotado** can also mean *sold out*: **las entradas están agotadas** (the tickets are sold out) — same verb, different context.
**agotador/a** = exhausting: **fue un día agotador** (it was an exhausting day).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm exhausted after the run.
cards.phrase: Estoy agotado después de correr.

cards.grammarNote:
**curioso/a** = curious — can describe a person or a thing (meaning *strange/interesting*).
Use **estar** for the current emotional state: **estoy curioso por eso** (I'm curious about that).
Use **ser** for personality: **es una persona muy curiosa** (she's a very curious person).
Also: **tener curiosidad** = to be curious: **tengo mucha curiosidad por saber** (I'm very curious to know).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm curious about that.
cards.phrase: Estoy curioso por eso.

cards.grammarNote:
**doler** (to hurt) works like **gustar** — the body part is the grammatical subject
**Me duele la cabeza** (singular) · **Me duelen los pies** (plural)
The pronoun **me/te/le** indicates who is hurting
cards.englishPhrase: My head hurts.
cards.phrase: Me duele la cabeza.

cards.grammarNote:
**el pelo** is the everyday word for hair (on the head); **el cabello** is more formal/literary.
In the phrase **Ella tiene el pelo largo**, the definite article **el** is used instead of a possessive — Spanish describes physical characteristics this way: **tiene los ojos azules** (she has blue eyes), **tiene la nariz pequeña** (he has a small nose).
cards.englishPhrase: She has long hair.
cards.phrase: Ella tiene el pelo largo.

cards.grammarNote:
**Lávate la cara** is a reflexive command (tú form): **lávate** = wash yourself.
With body-care reflexive verbs, use the **definite article** (**la cara**, **las manos**) not a possessive (**tu cara**).
The reflexive pronoun **te** already shows whose face it is.
Formal command (usted): **Lávese la cara**.
cards.englishPhrase: Wash your face.
cards.phrase: Lávate la cara.

cards.grammarNote:
Paired body parts use the plural with the definite article: **los ojos** (eyes), **las manos** (hands), **los pies** (feet), **los oídos** (ears).
Spanish describes eye color with **tener + los + body part + adjective**: **Él tiene los ojos azules** — literally 'he has the eyes blue.' The adjective follows the noun and agrees in gender and number.
cards.englishPhrase: He has blue eyes.
cards.phrase: Él tiene los ojos azules.

cards.grammarNote:
Spanish has two words for ear: **la oreja** (the outer, visible ear) and **el oído** (the inner ear / sense of hearing).
**Me duele la oreja** = my outer ear hurts · **Tengo el oído tapado** = my inner ear is blocked.
**doler** works like **gustar**: the body part is the subject, **me** is the indirect object pronoun.
cards.englishPhrase: My ear hurts.
cards.phrase: Me duele la oreja.

cards.grammarNote:
**Tengo la nariz fría** uses **tener + definite article + body part + adjective** to describe a physical state.
This pattern is very common: **tengo el cuello rígido** (my neck is stiff), **tengo la pierna cansada** (my leg is tired).
Contrast with **me duele** for pain: **me duele la nariz** (my nose hurts).
cards.englishPhrase: My nose is cold.
cards.phrase: Tengo la nariz fría.

cards.grammarNote:
**Abre la boca** is an informal (tú) imperative. Regular -ar verbs form the tú command with the él/ella present form: **abr-e**.
The formal (usted) command is **Abra la boca** — note the vowel switch: -ar verbs use -e for formal commands.
Note the definite article **la** — not *tu boca*.
cards.englishPhrase: Open your mouth.
cards.phrase: Abre la boca.

cards.grammarNote:
Paired body parts use the plural with definite article: **los labios** (lips), not *sus labios* when describing a person's physical features.
**Tiene los labios rojos** — the adjective **rojos** agrees in gender (masculine) and number (plural) with **labios**.
This **tener + los/las + body part + adjective** structure describes physical appearance.
cards.englishPhrase: She has red lips.
cards.phrase: Tiene los labios rojos.

cards.grammarNote:
**doler** works like **gustar** — the tooth is the grammatical subject: **Me duele un diente** (a tooth is hurting me).
Note **un** (indefinite article) instead of **el** here — 'a tooth' (one in particular, but not previously specified).
For general toothache: **tener dolor de muelas** (to have a toothache) — **muela** refers specifically to a molar.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a toothache.
cards.phrase: Me duele un diente.

cards.grammarNote:
**la lengua** means both 'tongue' (body part) and 'language' in Spanish: **hablar una lengua** (to speak a language).
**Saca la lengua** — **sacar** (to take out / stick out) is an informal tú command. Note the definite article **la** instead of a possessive.
For the formal command: **Saque la lengua**.
cards.englishPhrase: Stick out your tongue.
cards.phrase: Saca la lengua.

cards.grammarNote:
**el cuello** means both 'neck' (body part) and 'collar/neckline' of a garment.
**Tengo el cuello rígido** uses **tener + el + body part + adjective** for physical states.
For pain: **Me duele el cuello** (my neck hurts) using the **doler** + gustar pattern.
**rígido** (stiff/rigid) agrees in gender with **cuello** (masculine).
cards.englishPhrase: My neck is stiff.
cards.phrase: Tengo el cuello rígido.

cards.grammarNote:
**Me rompí el brazo** — reflexive verb (**romper** → **romperse**) with the definite article, not a possessive.
The reflexive pronoun **me** shows it's my own arm; **el** replaces *mi*.
This pattern applies to all injury verbs: **me torcí el tobillo** (I sprained my ankle), **me corté el dedo** (I cut my finger).
**rompí** is preterite (past): **romper** → rompí, rompiste, rompió, rompimos, rompieron.
cards.englishPhrase: I broke my arm.
cards.phrase: Me rompí el brazo.

cards.grammarNote:
With reflexive verbs and body parts, use the definite article instead of a possessive:
**Lávate las manos** (not *lava tus manos*) · **Me rompí el brazo** (I broke my arm)
The reflexive pronoun **me/te/se** makes clear whose body part it is
cards.englishPhrase: Wash your hands.
cards.phrase: Lávate las manos.

cards.grammarNote:
Spanish uses **el dedo** for both finger and toe. To distinguish:
**el dedo de la mano** (finger) · **el dedo del pie** (toe).
**Se cortó el dedo** — reflexive **cortarse** (to cut oneself) with definite article instead of possessive.
The reflexive pronoun **se** shows it was his own finger; **el** replaces *su*.
cards.englishPhrase: He cut his finger.
cards.phrase: Se cortó el dedo.

cards.grammarNote:
**tener dolor en** + body part = to have pain in a body part: **tiene dolor en el pecho** (he has chest pain).
Alternative: **tener dolor de** + body part for common ailments: **dolor de cabeza** (headache), **dolor de espalda** (back pain), **dolor de estómago** (stomachache).
**el pecho** can also refer to the breast area generally; **el seno** is more specific for breast.
cards.englishPhrase: He has chest pain.
cards.phrase: Él tiene dolor en el pecho.

cards.grammarNote:
**doler** works like **gustar**: **Me duele la espalda** — literally 'the back hurts to me.'
For specific regions: **la parte baja de la espalda** (lower back) · **la parte alta de la espalda** (upper back).
