**Usa** = tú affirmative imperative of **usar** (to use). Regular -ar: **usas** → **usa**. This command is critical in D&D: **¡Usa la poción de vida!** (Use the health potion!) can save a character.

**Cúralo** = ¡Cura! + direct object pronoun **lo** (him/it) attached to the end of the imperative — affirmative commands attach pronouns as suffixes. The accent on **cú-** preserves the original stress: **cura** + **lo** = **cúralo**.

**Defiéndete** = ¡Defiende! (stem-changing e→ie) + reflexive pronoun **te** attached. Accent added to preserve stress: **defiende** + **te** = **defiéndete**. The e→ie stem change applies in the tú imperative.
**Sube** = tú affirmative imperative of **subir** (regular -ir). The tú present is **subes** → drop -s → **sube**. The full phrase **¡Sube de nivel!** (Level up!) is used in Spanish D&D communities.

cards.word:
di (decir) · haz (hacer) · ve (ir/ver) · pon (poner)
sal (salir) · sé (ser) · ten (tener) · ven (venir)
cards.grammarNote: These 8 verbs have irregular tú imperative forms that don't follow the 'drop the -s' rule. In D&D: **¡Ten cuidado!** (Be careful!) · **¡Ven aquí!** (Come here!) · **¡Sal de ahí!** (Get out of there!) · **¡Haz algo!** (Do something!)

**Ten** = tú affirmative imperative of **tener** (irregular — one of the 8). **¡Ten cuidado!** (Be careful!) is one of the most useful phrases in D&D and everyday Spanish. Full phrase: **¡Ten cuidado con las trampas!** (Watch out for the traps!)

Nosotros commands use the nosotros subjunctive form: **atacar → ataquemos**. However, **vamos a + infinitive** (Let's go to / Let's [do]) is more common in everyday speech: **¡Vamos a explorar la mazmorra!** (Let's explore the dungeon!)

Ustedes commands use the ustedes subjunctive form: **atacar → ataquen** (c→qu before e). Jeffrey uses ustedes commands when directing the whole party: **¡Ataquen al dragón!** (Attack the dragon!), **¡Huyan!** (Flee!)

Negative tú commands always use the present subjunctive — never the affirmative imperative form. **muevas** = tú present subjunctive of **moverse** (o→ue: mueva, muevas…). Pronoun placement with negative commands: before the verb (**no te muevas**), unlike affirmative commands where pronouns attach after (**¡muévete!**).

cards.english:
Full battle command sequence:
'Attack! Don't flee! Use the potion!'
cards.grammarNote: Mix of affirmative and negative commands: **¡Ataca!** (affirmative tú) · **¡No huyas!** (negative tú — uses subjunctive **huyas**) · **¡Usa la poción!** (affirmative tú). This is the grammar of D&D combat narration in Spanish.

cards.english: Tell us everything you know. (usted command — to innkeeper)
cards.grammarNote: Usted commands use the subjunctive: **contar** (o→ue) → usted subjunctive **cuente** → **cuéntenos** (with indirect object pronoun **nos** attached). **Todo lo que sabe** = everything you know — **lo que** = what (relative pronoun introducing a clause).

cards.word:
uno · dos · tres · cuatro · cinco
seis · siete · ocho · nueve · diez
cards.grammarNote: **Uno** becomes **un** before a masculine noun: **un dado** (one die). Before a feminine noun: **una cara** (one face/side). Numbers 2–10 are invariable (no gender change).

cards.word:
once · doce · trece · catorce · quince
dieciséis · diecisiete · dieciocho · diecinueve · veinte
cards.grammarNote: 11–15 are unique forms. 16–19 combine **diez** + **y** + unit, contracted into one word: **dieciséis** (diez y seis), **diecisiete**, etc. **Veinte** (20) is its own form. The critical D&D roll: **¡Tiré un veinte!** (I rolled a twenty!)

cards.word:
veinte · treinta · cuarenta · cincuenta
sesenta · setenta · ochenta · noventa · cien
cards.grammarNote: 21–29 are written as one word: **veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés…** 31–99 use **y**: **treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco**. **Cien** = exactly 100; **ciento** is used before other numbers: **ciento cincuenta** (150).

cards.word:
cien(to) · doscientos · trescientos · cuatrocientos · quinientos
seiscientos · setecientos · ochocientos · novecientos · mil
cards.grammarNote: Hundreds 200–900 agree in gender with the noun they modify: **doscientos puntos** (m.) but **doscientas fichas** (f.). Note irregular forms: **quinientos** (500), **setecientos** (700), **novecientos** (900) — not **cincocientos** etc.

**Saqué** = I got/rolled — preterite yo of **sacar** (c→qu before e: saqué). **Tiré** = I threw/rolled — preterite yo of **tirar** (regular -ar: tiré). Both verbs are used colloquially for rolling dice in Spanish D&D communities.

cards.english: I need a six or higher.
cards.grammarNote: **o más** = or more/higher — **más** (more) functions as a comparison word. Alternative: **Necesito un seis como mínimo** (I need at least a six — literally 'as a minimum'). **como mínimo** / **al menos** = at least.

**cincuenta** = 50 (invariable — numbers from 2 upward don't change for gender). **Tengo** is the irregular yo form of **tener** (to have). Useful D&D health phrases: **Me quedan diez puntos de vida** (I only have ten hit points left — lit. 'there remain to me ten').

cards.word: El dragón hace veinticinco puntos de daño.
cards.grammarNote: **hace** = deals/does (él/ella present of **hacer**, irregular yo: **hago**). **Puntos de daño** = damage points — the standard D&D phrase in Spanish. **veinticinco** = 25 (written as one word, like all 21–29).

cards.word:
el d4 · el d6 · el d8 · el d10 · el d12 · el d20 · el d100
OR: dado de cuatro caras, dado de seis caras…
cards.grammarNote: Spanish D&D communities often borrow the English abbreviations (d4, d6, d20) directly. The descriptive form is **dado de [number] caras** (die of [number] faces). All are masculine: **el dado**, **los dados**.

cards.english:
Ordinal numbers 1st–10th
(for rounds, levels, dungeon floors)
cards.word:
primero/a · segundo/a · tercero/a · cuarto/a · quinto/a
sexto/a · séptimo/a · octavo/a · noveno/a · décimo/a
cards.grammarNote: Ordinals agree in gender: **el primer nivel** (the first level — **primero** drops -o before masculine nouns), **la tercera planta** (the third floor). Above 10th, cardinal numbers are commonly used instead: **el nivel once** (level eleven).

cards.word: El explorador de Jeffrey es nivel ocho.
cards.grammarNote: **es nivel ocho** — in D&D, level is treated as an identity characteristic (ser). Note: no article before **nivel** in this construction: **es nivel ocho** (not 'el nivel ocho'). Compare: **Estamos en el nivel ocho** (We are on level eight — estar for location).

cards.english: I rolled a fourteen for initiative.
cards.grammarNote: **catorce** = 14 (unique form, not **diezycuatro**). **de iniciativa** = for initiative — **de** links the roll to its purpose. Full D&D initiative sequence: **Todos tiran iniciativa** → **¿Cuánto sacaste?** (What did you roll?) → **Saqué un catorce** (I got a fourteen).

cards.english: That's eight plus four, so twelve total.
cards.word: Son ocho más cuatro, entonces doce en total.
cards.grammarNote: Math language in Spanish: **más** = plus, **menos** = minus, **por** = times/multiplied by, **entre** = divided by. **Son** (from **ser**) is used for sums and totals: **Tres más tres son seis** (Three plus three is six). **en total** = in total / altogether.

cards.english: We found three hundred gold coins.
cards.grammarNote: **trescientas** — note the feminine form agreeing with **monedas** (coins, feminine): **trescientos** (m.) vs **trescientas** (f.). All hundreds from 200–900 have masculine and feminine forms. **monedas de oro** = gold coins (literally 'coins of gold').

cards.english: When do you use the preterite in Spanish?
cards.word:
Use the preterite for completed past actions with a definite start/end — the main narrative tense for storytelling.
Examples: El dragón atacó. Encontramos el tesoro. Jeffrey lanzó el hechizo.
cards.grammarNote: The preterite (pretérito indefinido) is the go-to tense for D&D storytelling — each completed action in the adventure is in the preterite. Contrast with the imperfect (pretérito imperfecto), which describes ongoing states or background conditions.

cards.english:
Preterite endings for regular -AR verbs
(e.g. atacar → but note spelling change!)
cards.word:
-é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron
tirar: tiré, tiraste, tiró, tiramos, tirasteis, tiraron
lanzar (yo): lancé (z→c before e)
cards.grammarNote: -AR verbs add these endings to the stem. Key spelling changes in the yo form: c→qu (atacar → ataqué), z→c (lanzar → lancé), g→gu (llegar → llegué). Other persons are regular.

cards.english:
Preterite endings for regular -ER/-IR verbs
(e.g. comer, subir)
cards.word:
-í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron
comer: comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron
subir: subí, subiste, subió, subimos, subisteis, subieron
cards.grammarNote: -ER and -IR verbs share the same preterite endings. Note: -IR stem-changing verbs (e→i, o→u) apply the stem change in the él/ella and ellos forms only: **pedir → pidió, pidieron** (not in yo/tú/nosotros).

cards.english:
The dragon attacked the party.
(preterite narrative)
cards.grammarNote: **atacó** = he/she/it attacked — él/ella preterite of **atacar** (regular, no spelling change in third person). The yo form has the spelling change: **ataqué** (c→qu before e).

**Encontramos** = we found — nosotros preterite of **encontrar** (regular -ar). Note: the nosotros preterite of -ar verbs is identical to the nosotros present: **encontramos** = we find / we found. Context determines the tense.

cards.english:
Jeffrey cast a fire spell.
(preterite narrative)
cards.word: Jeffrey lanzó un hechizo de fuego.
cards.grammarNote: **lanzó** = he cast/threw — él/ella preterite of **lanzar** (regular in third person). The yo form has spelling change: **lancé** (z→c before e).

cards.english:
Preterite of SER (to be) and IR (to go)
[they share the same forms!]
cards.word:
fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron
(same for both SER and IR — context clarifies meaning)
cards.grammarNote: **Fue** can mean 'he was' (ser) or 'he went' (ir) — only context tells you which. D&D examples: **El dragón fue derrotado** (The dragon was defeated — ser/passive) vs **El grupo fue a la mazmorra** (The group went to the dungeon — ir).

cards.word: hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron
cards.grammarNote: **hacer** has a completely irregular preterite. Note: **hizo** (él/ella form) uses z instead of c to preserve the soft /s/ sound before o. D&D context: **Jeffrey hizo un golpe crítico** (Jeffrey made a critical hit). **¿Qué hiciste?** (What did you do?)

cards.word: tuve, tuviste, tuvo, tuvimos, tuvisteis, tuvieron
cards.grammarNote: **tener** in the preterite often means 'got/obtained' rather than just 'had': **Tuve suerte** (I got lucky / I was lucky). D&D context: **Tuvimos éxito en la misión** (We succeeded in the quest — we had success).

cards.english: Preterite of PODER (to be able to)
cards.word: pude, pudiste, pudo, pudimos, pudisteis, pudieron
cards.grammarNote: **poder** in the preterite means 'managed to' (succeeded in doing something). D&D: **El explorador pudo disparar antes de que el dragón atacara** (The ranger managed to shoot before the dragon attacked).

cards.english:
The goblin died after two hits.
(-IR stem-changing verb in preterite)
cards.word: El duende murió después de dos golpes.
cards.grammarNote: **murió** = he/she died — preterite of **morir** (o→u stem change in él/ella and ellos preterite forms only): morí, moriste, **murió**, morimos, moristeis, **murieron**. This o→u shift applies to **-IR** verbs with o→ue or o→u in the present.

cards.english:
Jeffrey asked his brother to roll initiative.
(-IR e→i verb in preterite)
cards.word: Jeffrey le pidió a su hermano que tirara la iniciativa.
cards.grammarNote: **pidió** = he asked/requested — preterite of **pedir** (e→i stem change in él/ella and ellos forms): pedí, pediste, **pidió**, pedimos, pedisteis, **pidieron**. Other -IR e→i verbs: **servir → sirvió**, **reír → rió**, **elegir → eligió**.

cards.english:
Narrate a battle in preterite:
First… then… finally…
cards.word:
Primero, el guerrero atacó al duende.
Luego, el mago lanzó un hechizo.
Finalmente, Jeffrey derrotó al dragón con una flecha.
cards.grammarNote: Sequence markers for preterite narratives: **primero** (first), **luego / después** (then/later), **finalmente / por fin** (finally/at last). These are the building blocks of D&D storytelling in Spanish.

cards.english:
We climbed the mountain. / We climb the mountain.
(nosotros preterite vs present — -AR verbs)
cards.word:
Subimos la montaña.
(same form for both present and preterite!)
cards.grammarNote: For -AR verbs, the nosotros preterite and present are identical: **subimos** = we climb / we climbed. Context (especially time markers) determines the tense: **Ayer subimos la montaña** (Yesterday we climbed) vs **Cada día subimos la montaña** (Every day we climb).

cards.english: SER vs ESTAR — what's the core difference?
cards.word:
SER = inherent/permanent identity, characteristics, origin, roles
ESTAR = temporary states, conditions, location, emotions

El dragón ES poderoso. (inherent trait)
El dragón ESTÁ herido. (temporary condition)
cards.grammarNote: Both **ser** and **estar** mean 'to be' in English, but they are not interchangeable. In D&D, you use **ser** to describe what something fundamentally is (class, origin, nature) and **estar** for its current state in battle or story.

cards.english:
Jeffrey is a dungeon master.
(SER — identity/role)
cards.word: Jeffrey es el director del juego.
cards.grammarNote: **es** (ser) for roles and identities — being the DM is Jeffrey's function and identity for the session. Compare: **Jeffrey está cansado** (Jeffrey is tired — estar, temporary state).

cards.english:
The wizard is from the northern kingdom.
(SER — origin)
cards.word: El mago es del reino del norte.
cards.grammarNote: **ser + de** = to be from (origin). **del** = de + el (mandatory contraction). Origin is always **ser**, never **estar**: **¿De dónde eres?** (Where are you from?) uses **ser**.

cards.english:
The dragon is powerful and ancient.
(SER — inherent nature)
cards.word: El dragón es poderoso y antiguo.
cards.grammarNote: **es** (ser) for inherent, permanent characteristics of the dragon — power and age are fundamental traits, not temporary states. Compare battle damage: **El dragón está debilitado** (The dragon is weakened — estar, current condition).

cards.english:
The warrior is wounded.
(ESTAR — temporary condition)
cards.grammarNote: **está herido** = is wounded — **estar** for the current physical state resulting from battle. **herido** is a past participle used as adjective (agrees masculine with **guerrero**). When healed, this state changes: **El guerrero ya no está herido** (The warrior is no longer wounded).

cards.english:
The dungeon is to the north.
(ESTAR — location)
cards.grammarNote: **está** (estar) for location — all locations use **estar** (except events: **La fiesta es en la taberna** — ser for where events take place). **al norte** = to the north (al = a + el).

cards.english:
Jeffrey is excited about the campaign.
(ESTAR — emotion/state)
cards.word: Jeffrey está emocionado con la campaña.
cards.grammarNote: **estar** for emotions and feelings — they are temporary states that change. **emocionado** agrees masculine with Jeffrey. Compare: **Jeffrey es apasionado** (Jeffrey is passionate — ser, a character trait he always has).

cards.english:
The goblin is dead.
(ESTAR — resulting state)
vs. the goblin is mortal
(SER — inherent nature)
cards.word:
El duende está muerto. (current state — dead)
El duende es mortal. (inherent nature — mortal)
cards.grammarNote: **estar muerto** = is dead (current state — even 'dead' is treated as a temporary condition with estar!). **ser mortal** = is mortal (inherent characteristic). This is a classic ser/estar contrast: the state of being dead (estar) vs the nature of being mortal (ser).

cards.english:
My character is a ranger.
(SER — class/identity)
cards.grammarNote: **es** (ser) for character class — this is an identity/category. Compare a temporary role: **Mi personaje está al frente** (My character is at the front — estar, location/position in combat).

cards.english:
The party is ready to attack.
(ESTAR — readiness state)
cards.word: El grupo está listo para atacar.
cards.grammarNote: **está listo** = is ready — **estar** for the current state of readiness. Note: **listo** with **ser** means 'clever/smart': **El mago es muy listo** (The wizard is very clever). The ser/estar contrast changes the meaning of **listo** entirely.

cards.english:
The sword is enchanted.
(ESTAR — resulting state from magic)
cards.grammarNote: **está encantada** — **estar** for a state produced by an action (enchanting). Past participles used as adjectives after **estar** describe resulting states: **está rota** (is broken), **está maldita** (is cursed), **está encantada** (is enchanted).

cards.english:
SER vs ESTAR changes meaning with some adjectives:
aburrido, malo, bueno, listo, seguro
cards.word:
ES aburrido = he IS boring (personality)
ESTÁ aburrido = he IS bored (right now)
ES malo = he is evil/bad (nature)
ESTÁ malo = he is sick (condition)
ES listo = he is clever · ESTÁ listo = he is ready
cards.grammarNote: Some adjectives change meaning entirely depending on whether they follow **ser** or **estar**. This is one of the most important ser/estar distinctions. D&D example: **El dragón es malo** (The dragon is evil) vs **El guerrero está malo** (The warrior is sick/ill).

cards.english:
Describe the dungeon using both SER and ESTAR:
'The dungeon is ancient. It is also dark right now.'
cards.word: La mazmorra es antigua. También está oscura.
cards.grammarNote: **es antigua** = is ancient (ser — permanent, inherent age). **está oscura** = is dark (estar — current condition, could change if you light a torch). This contrast perfectly illustrates ser (what something essentially is) vs estar (what it's like right now).

cards.english: When do you use the subjunctive in Spanish?
cards.word:
Use the subjunctive after expressions of wish, desire, need, emotion, or doubt — especially when two different subjects are involved.
Key triggers: querer que, necesitar que, esperar que, pedir que
cards.grammarNote: The subjunctive is a mood, not a tense. It expresses subjectivity — things wished for, feared, doubted, or commanded — rather than objective facts.

cards.english:
Present subjunctive: yo form of -AR verbs
(e.g. atacar → ataque)
cards.word:
Start from the yo indicative → drop -o → add opposite vowel endings
ataco → atac- → ataque
tirar → tiro → tire
lanzar → lanzo → lance
cards.grammarNote: The subjunctive of -AR verbs uses -e endings (the 'opposite' of the indicative -a endings). Spelling changes that appear in the yo indicative carry into the subjunctive: atacar → ataco → ataque (c→qu).

cards.english:
Present subjunctive: yo form of -ER/-IR verbs
(e.g. correr → corra, subir → suba)
cards.word:
Start from yo indicative → drop -o → add opposite vowel endings (-a)
corro → corr- → corra
subo → sub- → suba
curo → cur- → cure
cards.grammarNote: -ER and -IR verbs use -a endings in the subjunctive (opposite of their indicative -e endings). Irregular yo forms carry through: tener → tengo → tenga; hacer → hago → haga.

cards.english:
I want the wizard to cast a spell.
(querer que + subjunctive)
cards.word: Quiero que el mago lance un hechizo.
cards.grammarNote: **querer que + subjunctive** = to want someone to do something. Two different subjects require the subjunctive: 'I' want, 'the wizard' casts. If the subject is the same, use infinitive: **Quiero lanzar un hechizo** (I want to cast a spell).

cards.english:
I need you to roll the dice.
(necesitar que + subjunctive)
cards.grammarNote: **necesitar que + subjunctive** = to need someone to do something. **tires** = tú present subjunctive of **tirar**: tire, tires, tire, tiremos, tiréis, tiren.

cards.english:
I hope the paladin survives.
(esperar que + subjunctive)
cards.grammarNote: **esperar que + subjunctive** = to hope that… **sobreviva** is the subjunctive of **sobrevivir** (to survive): sobrevivo → sobreviva.

cards.english:
Jeffrey asks his brothers to be quiet during the narration.
(pedir que + subjunctive)
cards.word: Jeffrey les pide que estén callados durante la narración.
cards.grammarNote: **pedir que + subjunctive** = to ask/request that someone do something. **estén** is the subjunctive of **estar**: esté, estés, esté, estemos, estéis, estén — irregular because **estar** has an irregular yo form (**estoy → esté**).

cards.word: haga, hagas, haga, hagamos, hagáis, hagan
cards.grammarNote: **hacer** has an irregular yo: **hago** → subjunctive stem **hag-** + subjunctive endings. Context: **Necesito que el guerrero haga algo** (I need the warrior to do something).

cards.word: tenga, tengas, tenga, tengamos, tengáis, tengan
cards.grammarNote: **tener** irregular yo: **tengo** → subjunctive stem **teng-** + endings. Context: **Quiero que el grupo tenga más puntos de vida** (I want the party to have more hit points).

cards.english: Subjunctive of PODER (to be able to)
cards.word: pueda, puedas, pueda, podamos, podáis, puedan
cards.grammarNote:
**poder** is o→ue stem-changing; this carries into the subjunctive for all forms except nosotros and vosotros: **pueda** (yo), **podamos** (nosotros).
Context: **Espero que el mago pueda curar al guerrero** (I hope the wizard can heal the warrior).

cards.word: sea, seas, sea, seamos, seáis, sean
cards.grammarNote: **ser** is fully irregular in the subjunctive — no connection to the yo indicative form (**soy**). Context: **Quiero que la campaña sea épica** (I want the campaign to be epic).

cards.word: esté, estés, esté, estemos, estéis, estén
cards.grammarNote: **estar** subjunctive adds a written accent on all forms except nosotros/vosotros. Context: **Necesito que el guerrero esté listo** (I need the warrior to be ready).

cards.english:
I hope Jeffrey rolls a twenty!
(ojalá + subjunctive)
cards.grammarNote:
**Ojalá (que) + subjunctive** = I hope / If only — from Arabic **law sha' Allah** (if God wills). No additional trigger verb is needed; **ojalá** stands alone and always takes the subjunctive.
**saque** = subjunctive of **sacar** (c→qu before e): saque, saques, saque…

cards.english:
I want the ranger to attack first.
(D&D battle scenario)
cards.word: Quiero que el explorador ataque primero.
cards.grammarNote: **ataque** = tú/él/ella present subjunctive of **atacar** (c→qu before e). Battle commands to other party members through Jeffrey as DM: **quiero que + subjunctive** tells someone what role they should play.

cards.english:
The party needs the wizard to heal everyone.
(D&D healing scenario)
cards.word: El grupo necesita que el mago cure a todos.
cards.grammarNote:
**cure** = subjunctive of **curar** (regular -ar): cure, cures, cure, curemos, curéis, curen.
**a todos** = everyone — **personal a** + **todos** (all/everyone). The personal **a** is used before human direct objects.
